analysis.one_liner: Caps greenhouse gas emissions, requires rising renewable electricity, and tightens vehicle pollution standards.
analysis.headline: Backed by 113 cosponsors including 6 Republicans, the climate bill never received a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to set annual targets cutting U.S. greenhouse gas emissions about 2% a year starting in 2011, returning emissions to 1990 levels by 2020 and to 20% of 1990 levels by 2050. It would enforce those targets with a cap-and-trade system covering the largest emitters, with allowances mostly auctioned and the proceeds going to a Climate Reinvestment Fund to cushion energy costs for low-income households and help affected workers. It also would have required vehicle emissions standards at least as strict as California's 2004 rules, 20% of retail electricity from renewable sources by 2020, and rising annual efficiency savings from electric and gas utilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households gain the most: less exposure to the climate damages the bill's own findings describe — heat waves, drought, stronger hurricanes, and sea-level rise — plus utility efficiency mandates that cut bills, auction revenue earmarked to shield low-income customers from energy price increases, and transition aid for workers and regions dependent on high-carbon energy. Renewable electricity producers gain a guaranteed market growing to 20% of U.S. retail sales by 2020.

how_it_helps.text: Requires annual emission targets that bring U.S. greenhouse gas emissions back to 1990 levels by 2020 and down to 20% of 1990 levels by 2050, enforced through caps on the largest-emitting sources and sectors.

Sells allowances mainly by auction and deposits the proceeds, plus penalties, in a Climate Reinvestment Fund dedicated to mitigating energy cost increases — particularly for low-income consumers — and to providing transition assistance to workers and regions moving away from high-carbon energy.
Requires vehicle greenhouse gas standards at least as strict as the California Air Resources Board's September 2004 standards, tightening every five years after 2014.

Requires retail electricity to include at least 20% renewable energy by 2020 and sets cumulative end-user efficiency savings targets on electric and gas suppliers, rising to 1% of sales per year — savings that show up directly on customers' bills.

Builds in anti-giveaway guards: allowances are explicitly not property rights, free allocations cannot create windfall profits for covered polluters, and excess emissions draw a civil penalty equal to twice the allowance market price. State climate laws remain untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and gas-fired power plants and other large emitters would pay for allowances at auction, cut their emissions, and face civil penalties at twice the permit price for exceeding the cap. Automakers and oil refiners would bear the cost of meeting California-level vehicle standards. Some compliance costs would reach consumers through higher energy prices, though the bill directs auction revenue toward blunting that impact, especially for low-income households, and toward helping displaced energy workers.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs from the cap and the renewable and efficiency mandates would partly reach households as higher electricity, heating, and fuel prices; the bill offsets this with auction-funded aid to low-income consumers, but the Climate Reinvestment Fund depends on annual appropriations, so the cushion is not automatic.

The required cuts are deep on a short timeline — back to 1990 levels within roughly a decade of the cap starting — which would force rapid replacement of fossil generation and impose a costly transition on coal-dependent utilities, mining regions, and their workers, even with the bill's transition-assistance fund.

Allowances can be held and traded by any person, creating a new commodity market in pollution permits with room for price volatility and speculation, and the cap itself does not begin binding until 2010 with EPA regulations due two years after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacked a century-scale risk with unusually hard tools: fixed annual targets, mostly auctioned permits rather than free giveaways, penalties at twice the market price, and no preemption of stricter state laws. The real costs would fall on fossil-fuel generators and partly on energy bills, cushioned for the households least able to pay them and paired with transition aid for the workers and regions the policy would hurt. The design's main weaknesses are the appropriations-dependent consumer cushion and the tradable-permit market it creates. On balance it was a serious, consumer-protective attempt at deep emission cuts whose costs are real but smaller and more concentrated than the climate damages it aimed to prevent.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in June 2006 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, it was passed down to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee in July — and that is where it sat, with no hearing, markup, or vote, until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Safe Climate Act on June 20, 2006, joined by 14 original cosponsors including George Miller, Edward Markey, Frank Pallone, and Bernie Sanders.
The bill ultimately drew 113 cosponsors: 106 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 6 Republicans.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the International Relations Committee on the day of introduction.
On July 17, 2006, it was referred to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the Congress.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place; the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of coal- and gas-fired power plants, refiners, and other large emitters kept operating without emission caps, allowance auctions, or penalties, and automakers faced no new vehicle standards. Households got none of the bill's efficiency savings, low-income energy protections, or reduced climate risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large emitters that avoided caps and costs

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Climate Act with 14 original cosponsors and led it through the Congress.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only non-Democrats to sign on.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory limits on greenhouse gas emissions; his party controlled the House and the committee where the bill stalled.

sides.party_line_note: 107 of the 113 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent, only 6 were Republicans, and the Republican-controlled committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill caps their emissions, forces them to buy auctioned allowances or cut output, and fines excess emissions at twice the permit price, while the 20% renewable mandate and efficiency targets shrink the fossil share of the market. Their compliance costs are the bill's method of paying for consumer protections.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and the oil industry
industries.note: Refiners and other large fossil sources fall under the cap and auction system, and California-level vehicle standards would cut gasoline demand per mile. The cost of their emissions would start appearing on their own books rather than on the public.

They would have to meet fleetwide greenhouse gas standards at least as strict as California's 2004 rules, tightening every five years, requiring faster redesign of their vehicle lines. Consumers would recoup some of that in fuel savings.

The national standard requiring 20% renewable retail electricity by 2020, with annual increases starting in 2009, creates a guaranteed and growing market for wind, solar, and other renewable producers.

industries.industry: Coal regions and high-carbon energy workers
industries.note: The bill's cuts would shrink demand for high-carbon energy and the jobs that come with it, but it explicitly directs Climate Reinvestment Fund money to equitable transition assistance for affected workers and regions. The aid is real but depends on appropriations.
